emergency.notes: Tourist Police Headquarters Kathmandu: +977-1-444-4161. Emergency services can be slow in remote trekking areas. Carry a satellite communicator in high-altitude zones.
emergency.general: Call 100 for police or 102 for ambulance, though emergency response varies greatly by location. In Kathmandu, private hospitals often provide faster care than public emergency services. Outside major cities, medical evacuation may be necessary — operators primarily speak Nepali, so have your location details written down.

travelAdvisory.summary: Exercise increased caution in Nepal due to the potential for natural disasters including earthquakes and altitude-related medical emergencies. Political demonstrations may occur and can become violent. Trekking areas have limited emergency services.

travelAdvisoryUK.summary: Most visits to Nepal are trouble-free. Be aware of earthquake risk and altitude sickness risks during trekking. Check trail conditions before setting out. Political strikes (bandhs) may affect travel.

healthcare.systemType: Underdeveloped public system; private hospitals available in Kathmandu and Pokhara; minimal services in trekking regions
healthcare.costForTourists: Private clinic visit $20-60. Kathmandu private hospital $100-400/night. Emergency helicopter evacuation from trekking regions $3,000-15,000. Serious conditions require evacuation to Bangkok or New Delhi.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies available in Kathmandu and Pokhara. Limited in rural areas. Altitude sickness medication (acetazolamide) widely available without prescription.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: CIWEC Hospital and Grande International Hospital in Kathmandu recommended for tourists. In trekking regions, local health posts offer only basic care. Helicopter rescue is the primary emergency option at altitude.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Comprehensive travel insurance covering high-altitude helicopter evacuation is mandatory for trekking. TIMS (Trekkers' Information Management System) card required. Himalayan Rescue Association membership recommended.

pharmacy.hours: Pharmacies are widely available in Kathmandu and major towns, typically open 7am-9pm. Rural areas have very limited pharmacies. Many medications are available OTC in Nepal.
pharmacy.tips: Many common medications are available OTC, including some antibiotics and painkillers. Quality varies — use reputable pharmacies in Kathmandu. Generic medications are common. Bring all medications you might need, especially for trekking. Antimalarial medications are not widely available — bring your own.

vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for most travelers. Ensure routine vaccinations are current. Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, and Rabies are strongly recommended. Consider Japanese Encephalitis vaccination for extended rural stays near mosquitoes.

water.notes: Do NOT drink tap water in Nepal. Bottled water is essential — always drink sealed bottled water. Use bottled or purified water for brushing teeth. Water-borne diseases are common — be very careful.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Be very cautious with food. Eat at reputable restaurants in Kathmandu and Pokhara. Avoid raw vegetables and salads unless you're confident in the establishment. Only eat cooked foods served hot. Street food can cause serious issues. Dal bhat (lentil rice) at established restaurants is generally safe.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Highly recommended for all travelers. Mandatory for trekking in remote areas (many agencies require proof of insurance for treks). Medical evacuation insurance is critical.
travelInsurance.tips: Medical evacuation from remote trekking areas costs $15,000-50,000+ to Bangkok or Delhi. This is the single most important coverage. Even in Kathmandu, serious conditions may need evacuation. Public hospitals are inadequate for serious conditions. CIWEC Clinic in Kathmandu is the best option for tourists.

healthcare.qualityNotes: Healthcare quality is limited, especially outside Kathmandu. Kathmandu has several private hospitals and international clinics with decent care (Norvic Hospital, Sumeru Hospital, CIWEC Clinic). For serious conditions, medical evacuation to Bangkok or Delhi is required. Outside Kathmandu, facilities are very basic. Always carry your own medical supplies for trekking.

medications.prescriptionRules: Prescription requirements are not strictly enforced. For controlled substances, carry your prescription and doctor's letter. Nepali pharmacists are often helpful with common medication needs.

restrictedMeds.name: Diazepam (Valium) and benzodiazepines
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. Requires prescription. Carry your foreign prescription and doctor's letter. Quantities for personal use are permitted with documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled. Requires prescription. Bring your documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: Tramadol
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled opioid. Requires prescription. Bring your documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly controlled. Requires documentation and possibly Nepali doctor consultation. Contact your embassy if you need to travel with ADHD medications.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal in Nepal. Despite a historical tradition of cannabis use, it is now prohibited. Do not bring any cannabis products.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. This is critical for Nepal — bring all medications you might need for your entire trip. Supply chains are unreliable. For trekking, bring comprehensive medical supplies.
medications.generalAdvice: Nepal has limited pharmaceutical regulation and counterfeit medications are a concern, so bring sufficient supplies of any essential medications from home. Carry all prescriptions in original packaging with a doctor's letter. Controlled substances like strong painkillers and sedatives require clear documentation. For high-altitude trekking, consider bringing altitude sickness medication (acetazolamide) as availability outside Kathmandu is unreliable.

controlledSubstances.note: Prescription controlled under Narcotic Drugs Control Act 2033; available in pharmacies with prescription. Carry documentation for import
Amphetamines are controlled narcotics in Nepal; Adderall is not available and importation is prohibited
Illegal since 1973 under Narcotic Drugs Control Act despite historical cultural use; CBD products also prohibited
Controlled psychotropic substance; very limited availability in Nepal. Carry prescription and doctor's letter
Controlled under NDCA; codeine preparations available by prescription. Carry documentation and original packaging
Available in pharmacies; less strictly controlled than in many countries but carry original packaging for border crossing
Illegal narcotics under NDCA; penalties include imprisonment. Despite availability in tourist areas, legal risks are real
Controlled prescription medication; available in pharmacies with prescription. Carry documentation when importing
Prescription required under NDCA; importable with valid prescription for personal medical use

scams.name: Fake trekking permits and guides
scams.description: Touts sell fake TIMS cards, Annapurna/Everest entry permits, or offer guide services but abandon trekkers in remote areas after collecting payment.
scams.avoidance: Purchase all trekking permits only from official Nepal Tourism Board or authorized trekking agencies. Verify guide credentials and get receipts.

scams.name: Taxi flat-rate overcharging
scams.description: Drivers quote flat rates 3-5x the metered fare, especially from Tribhuvan Airport. Meters are deliberately broken.
scams.avoidance: Insist on using the meter, or pre-negotiate price. Kathmandu airport has prepaid taxi booths — use these.

scams.name: Gem and carpet scam
scams.description: Shopkeepers claim their gems, thangka paintings, or carpets are valuable antiques or rare minerals. Items are low-grade or entirely fake.
scams.avoidance: Do not buy gems or antiques for investment. Only purchase from government-certified shops. Never agree to 'resell on behalf of shop' schemes.

scams.name: Buddhist monastery donation scam
scams.description: Individuals posing as monks solicit donations for fake monasteries or orphanages. They use official-looking receipts.
scams.avoidance: Donate only to established, registered organizations. Verified monasteries do not typically solicit donations on the street.

scams.name: Restaurant/tea house overcharging on treks
scams.description: Tea houses quote lower prices for food and accommodation, then add hidden charges at checkout including service fees and gear rental surprises.
scams.avoidance: Agree on all prices (including service charge) before consuming or staying. Get written confirmation where possible.

connectivity.simOptions: Tourist SIMs from Ncell or Nepal Telecom at Tribhuvan Airport and major towns. $5-15 for data packages. Coverage good in Kathmandu/Pokhara, limited above 4,000m on treks. eSIM via Airalo (Ncell).
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Good in Kathmandu hotels and cafes. Available in most tea houses on Annapurna and EBC treks (paid). Very limited above 4,500m.
connectivity.bestOption: Ncell SIM for best data coverage in cities and lower trekking elevations. Consider satellite communicator (SPOT/Garmin inReach) for high-altitude emergencies.

cultural.tipping: Appreciated but not mandatory. Trekking guides: $10-20/day. Porters: $5-10/day. Restaurants: 10% or round up. Hotel staff: $1-2/bag.
cultural.dressCode: Dress modestly — cover shoulders and knees at temples and monasteries. Remove shoes before entering temples. Short sleeves acceptable in Kathmandu, but conservative dress shows respect.
cultural.greetings: Traditional greeting is 'Namaste' with palms pressed together and a slight bow. Sacred gesture showing respect. Do not use left hand for greeting or passing items.
taboos: Touching or pointing feet at sacred objects, shrines, or people
Clockwise is sacred — always walk clockwise around stupas and prayer wheels
Do not step over a person's head or legs (spiritually offensive)
Leather items may be prohibited in some Hindu temples
Public displays of affection are frowned upon
Disrespecting the king or religion can result in legal trouble
cultural.haggling: Expected at markets and with independent vendors. Fixed prices in established restaurants and shops. Trekking agencies and permit offices have fixed fees.

safety.lgbtSafety: Same-sex relationships were decriminalized in 2023 and Nepal has progressive laws for the region, including a third gender option. Acceptance varies widely between Kathmandu and rural areas.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Generally manageable with precautions. Stick to established trekking routes and hire reputable guides. Avoid walking alone after dark in cities. Verbal harassment can occur.
safety.notes: The primary risks for tourists are altitude sickness (above 3,000m), earthquakes, and trekking-related accidents. Kathmandu petty crime is common in Thamel. Nepal is generally friendly and welcoming to tourists.

practical.visaFreeCountries: Most nationalities require a visa. Available on arrival at Tribhuvan Airport or online at online.nepalimmigration.gov.np. 15/30/90 day options available for $30-100.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: October-November (post-monsoon, clear skies for Himalayan views) and March-May (spring, rhododendron blooms). Avoid June-September (monsoon, landslides). December-February is cold but crowd-free.

hospitals.name: CIWEC Hospital Travel Medicine Center
hospitals.notes: Specialist in travel medicine and altitude sickness. Preferred hospital for foreign visitors and trekkers.

hospitals.name: Grande International Hospital
hospitals.notes: Modern private hospital with good emergency facilities and English-speaking doctors.

hospitals.name: Western Regional Hospital Pokhara
hospitals.notes: Main hospital serving the Pokhara region and Annapurna trekking area. Basic facilities.

immediate: Drop, cover, and hold on under a sturdy table or against interior wall
Stay away from windows, exterior walls, and objects that may fall
If outdoors, move away from buildings, power lines, and trees
Do not use elevators after tremors — use stairs
after: Check for gas leaks — if smell of gas, evacuate and call fire service
Do not enter damaged buildings until cleared by authorities
Monitor Nepal Police and NDRRMA updates for aftershock warnings
Contact your embassy to register safety if communication disrupted
resources: NDRRMA (National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority): www.ndrrma.gov.np

immediate: At first symptoms (headache, nausea, dizziness above 2,500m): stop ascending immediately
Rest at current altitude for 24 hours and assess symptoms
Drink 4-6 liters of water per day
Take acetazolamide (Diamox) if previously prescribed for prevention
For severe symptoms (HACE/HAPE — confusion, extreme breathlessness): DESCEND IMMEDIATELY — minimum 500-1,000m
Contact helicopter rescue immediately for HACE or HAPE
after: Do not re-ascend until completely symptom-free for 24 hours
Consult CIWEC Hospital Travel Medicine if symptoms persist
Report incident to trekking agency and insurance provider
resources: Himalayan Rescue Association (HRA) Pheriche aid post: www.himalayanrescue.org
